title: The Trivial Pursuit Trivia Edition
summary: Hosts Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant cover the history of the board game Trivial Pursuit as a holiday gift pick: its origins in a Montreal apartment with Chris Haney and Scott Abbott, the early financing through the Horn Abbot Company, the Genus edition's 1981 launch, the boom of the mid-1980s in the US, legal disputes (David Wall lawsuit and Fred Worth's trick-question suit), and later editions. The episode closes with a listener mail about music streaming platforms like Bandcamp and SoundCloud.

segments.title: Opening banter and Trivial Pursuit as holiday pick
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the episode as a Christmas legendary gift pick and reminisce about playing Trivial Pursuit as kids.

segments.title: Trivia craze and Edwin Goodgold
segments.summary: Trivia quiz shows rose and fell over decades; Edwin Goodgold and Dan Carlinsky's 1960s trivia book and pub quizzes in England are discussed, along with the Jeopardy revival in 1984 and the name change to Trivial.

segments.title: Origins: Chris Haney and Scott Abbott
segments.summary: Two Canadian journalists, Chris Haney and Scott Abbott, came up with the game after a Scrabble session and decided to create a game.

segments.title: How the game is played
segments.summary: The hosts describe the circular pie-wedge board based on a ship's wheel, six categories, rolling the die, and the rules for winning, plus typical play length and team sizes.

segments.title: Name change and playing as a team
segments.summary: Sarah Haney suggested renaming the game from Trivia Pursuit to Trivial Pursuit; the hosts talk about family play and favorite categories.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Brief ad break mention between segments.

segments.title: Toy convention and forming the Horn Abbot Company
segments.summary: The inventors attended a Canadian toy trade show posing as reporters, found the board game industry closed and in a slump, and decided to self-produce; they formed Horn Abbot and sold shares to friends and family. Michael Wurstlin designed the artwork for shares.

segments.title: Writing questions and the Genus edition launch
segments.summary: They raised about forty thousand dollars plus a bank line of credit, wrote about six thousand questions in Spain in 1981, and launched the Genus edition in late 1981; major companies had passed, and Chaptain distributed the game.

segments.title: Sales boom and licensing to Selchow and Righter
segments.summary: Initial Canadian sales sold out before Christmas 1982; a US licensing deal with Selchow and Righter followed, and the game became a best seller and cost about double typical board games.

segments.title: Packaging and cultural adult appeal
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the elegant packaging, Alexander Pope quote on the box, the game's adult positioning, and its appeal to kids of 1980s parents.

segments.title: US boom, celebrity endorsements, and The Big Chill
segments.summary: US sales exploded in 1983-1984; the New York Times reported on trivia parties, Linda Pizzano sent the game to celebrities, and the cast of The Big Chill was reported playing it. Also a Saturday Night Live sketch parody is mentioned.

segments.title: Trivia books, Reagan anecdote, and sales totals
segments.summary: Robert J. Heller's book How to Win at Trivial Pursuit, Reagan playing the game, a Queen Elizabeth II tournament anecdote, and the spring 1985 household penetration figures are discussed along with lifetime sales estimates.

segments.title: Founders' fame and early investors
segments.summary: Haney and Abbott became celebrities and pitchmen; early investors like Susan Ferrier McKay and Wurstlin benefited financially.

segments.title: David Wall lawsuit
segments.summary: Australian David Wall sued in 1994 claiming Haney stole his idea after picking him up hitchhiking in Nova Scotia in 1979; the court ruled for Haney and awarded costs of about one million dollars after a thirteen-year battle.

segments.title: Fred Worth trick question lawsuit
segments.summary: Trivia author Fred Worth included a trick question about Columbo's first name, then sued for three hundred million dollars claiming nearly 1700 questions were his; a judge ruled facts cannot be copyrighted and dismissed the case. Hosts add a Columbo first-name aside.

segments.title: Founders' later ventures
segments.summary: In the 1990s the founders invested in racehorses, golf courses and the Brampton Battalion hockey team, which Abbott owned.

segments.title: Question writing process
segments.summary: Ron Rodriguez's role writing questions; the hosts describe the quota, the 45-character limit, and their own work supplying source material for the Stuff You Should Know edition.
topics: Stuff You Should Know Trivial Pursuit edition

segments.title: Later editions and gameplay evolution
segments.summary: Editions over time include Disney, Fame, Harry Potter-style niche versions, X, EMS, Trivial Pursuit Infinite, and a LeVar Burton CW show; the hosts debate whether specialist editions lost the game's way.

segments.title: Holiday sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts wrap the holiday pick and promise an upcoming holiday special.

segments.title: Listener mail: music streaming platforms
segments.summary: Listener Chris from Seattle writes about Bandcamp and SoundCloud being left out of the music streaming episode and how album lengths changed with the medium.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing credits and contact information.
